statement.p: Corn production, C, is a function of rainfall, R (in inches), and temperature, T (in degrees C). The first figure below shows how rainfall is predicted to vary with time because of global warming; the second, how temperature is predicted to vary with time because of global warming.
Graph of rainfall, R vs. time, t
Graph of temperature, T vs. time, t
Suppose that we know that (currently) \Delta C \approx 3.8 \Delta R - 5.1 \Delta T
Use this to estimate the change in corn production between the year 2020 and the year 2021.

static.solution:
R=15 inches and T=25^\circC, a change, \Delta R, in rainfall and a change, \Delta T, in temperature produces a change, \Delta C, in corn production given by \Delta C \approx 3.8 \Delta R - 5.1 \Delta T. Now both R and T are functions of time t (in years), and we want to find the effect of a small change in time, \Delta t, on R and T. The first figure shows that the slope of the graph for R versus t is about -0.7/10 = -0.07 in/year when t=2020. Similarly, the second shows the slope of the graph of T versus t is about 0.8/10 = 0.08^\circ C/year when t=2020. Thus, around the year 2020, \Delta R \approx -0.07 \Delta t \quad \mbox{ and} \quad \Delta T \approx 0.08 \Delta t.
Substituting these into the equation for \Delta C, we get \Delta C \approx (3.8)(-0.07) \Delta t - (5.1)(0.08) \Delta t \approx -0.674 \Delta t.
Thus in one year corn production will decline by about 0.674 in.
When t=2020 \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta t}\approx -0.674, so \frac{dC}{dt}\approx -0.674.
